scenario: AITA for not staying home and taking care of my sick wife all weekend? | On Thursday evening my wife started feeling unwell. I encouraged her to go to bed and told her I could handle the kids evening stuff by myself (3 kids, ages 9, 11, and 13). I checked on her after the kids were in bed at 9 and she was fevered- I asked if she wanted any medicine, made sure she had some water, and rubbed her back for a few minutes. I slept in the spare room but got up twice to check on her. The next morning I got the kids ready and off to school, went to a meeting and came home at 10 to take her to the doctor. I worked from home until our cleaning lady came around 1 and asked her to keep an eye on my wife and went back into the office for a couple meetings, picked up the kids and was home around 4. Her fever broke shortly after I got home at 4 and I helped her shower. Our oldest had a school dance and I got some movies and set the youngest 2 up in the den for the evening with pizza and some games so they'd be quiet. I checked on my wife periodically and after the oldest got home me and the 3 kids camped out in the den. On Saturday morning, the kids were restless so I took them out for the day bc I didn't want them to be around the house being loud. I checked on my wife and she was sleeping- I refilled her water and left her a note. Throughout the day I called and sent her messages and my mom took her over some homemade soup and checked on her. We were gone the majority of the day but the kids came home worn out and we crashed in the den again. I checked on my wife as soon as we got home and she was looking better. Sunday morning, the kids and I woke up early, did some yardwork then went to the store to do the weekly grocery shopping. When we got home my wife was up and about and still weak but feeling better. However, she was being really short with me and was in a bad mood. I thought it was just bc she didn't feel well but after a few hours of her making snide comments I asked her if something was wrong and she exploded on me that her family abandoned her while she was sick. She went off about how she always takes care of us when we're sick but we avoided her like the plague and didn't stay home and I made the cleaning lady and my mom take care of her instead of doing it myself. I tried to explain that I didn't want to expose the kids to being sick and I didn't want them around the house being loud while she was trying to rest and I checked on her multiple times. She said I should've sent the kids to my parents or something and stayed home and she can't believe I didn't sleep with her for 3 days. I starting getting angry and told her that I did what I thought was best and she sounded ungrateful bc it wasn't exactly what she would've done. She then called me an asshole. We went to bed angry and didn't really speak this morning. I keep stewing over this bc I don't think that I'm an asshole but maybe I am?

message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether the person in this scenario is being AITA (Ask if it's okay to ask) for not staying home and taking care of their sick wife all weekend. Let me break this down step by step. First, the situation: The wife starts feeling unwell on Thursday evening. The husband encourages her to rest, takes care of the kids, and checks on her. He sleeps in a spare room but gets up twice to check on her. The next day, he takes the kids to school, goes to a meeting, takes her to the doctor, works from home, and arranges for the cleaning lady to help. He also helps her shower when she feels better. On Saturday, he takes the kids out to avoid them being loud, checks on her, and sends messages. Sunday, they do yardwork and shopping, and when they get home, the wife is feeling better but is in a bad mood. She accuses him of abandoning her, not staying home, and not taking care of her properly, leading to an argument. So, the question is whether the husband is AITA for not staying home. Let me consider the possible perspectives. On one hand, the husband took several steps to ensure his wife was taken care of. He made sure she had medicine, water, and comfort. He arranged for the cleaning lady and his mom to check on her. He also took the kids out to give her peace. He was present when needed, helped her shower, and communicated with her throughout the day. He prioritized her rest by managing the kids and other responsibilities. On the other hand, the wife felt abandoned. She was expecting more direct care from him, like him staying home and not delegating tasks. She felt that he didn't prioritize her enough, especially since she usually takes care of the family when they're sick. She was upset that he didn't sleep with her and that he sent others to help instead. I think it's important to consider cultural and personal expectations here. In some cultures, it's expected for the husband to stay home and care for the sick wife, especially if she's the primary caregiver otherwise. The wife might feel that her role is being reversed, and she's not getting the same level of care she provides. However, the husband's approach was to manage the situation in a way that he thought was best, considering the kids and other responsibilities. He might have been trying to balance his duties without overexerting himself or the kids. He also didn't want to expose the kids to potential illness, which is a valid concern. The conflict arises from differing expectations. The husband did take actions to care for his wife, but perhaps not in the way she expected. She felt neglected because she wasn't getting the same level of attention she usually gives others. So, is the husband AITA? It depends on the context. If the wife expects him to stay home and provide direct care, then not doing so could be seen as not fulfilling his responsibilities. However, the husband's approach was also caring, just in a different way. He might not have been neglectful but rather handling things differently. In the end, communication seems to be the key issue. The husband and wife have different expectations about how care should be provided, and this led to conflict. It might be helpful for them to discuss their expectations and find a middle ground that works for both.
